prompt: Each activity below occurs in one stage of the consumption process. Sort them into Prepurchase, Purchase, and Postpurchase.

cards.text: A commuter notices her winter boots are leaking and compares waterproof ratings across three brands.
cards.explanation: In the prepurchase stage, the consumer recognizes a need, searches for information, and evaluates alternatives.

cards.text: A beverage company tests which package claims attract attention and build favorable attitudes before launch.
cards.explanation: In the prepurchase stage, the marketer studies how attitudes form and which cues attract attention.

cards.text: A shopper abandons an online order because the payment form requires creating an account.
cards.explanation: In the purchase stage, the consumer experiences the retail environment, time pressure, and payment process.

cards.text: A grocery retailer places cold beverages near the express register to reduce checkout friction.
cards.explanation: In the purchase stage, the marketer manages packaging, shelf placement, and checkout friction.

cards.text: After two weeks of daily use, a buyer decides his new desk lamp is too dim for reading.
cards.explanation: In the postpurchase stage, the consumer uses the item and evaluates whether it met expectations.

cards.text: An appliance brand tracks warranty claims, product returns, and repeat orders across retail channels.
cards.explanation: Postpurchase outcomes determine repeat sales, product returns, and word-of-mouth recommendations.

prompt: Match each market segmentation base with the company strategy that applies it.

pairs.match: A hardware chain stocks snow blowers in northern regions and dehumidifiers in humid coastal cities.
pairs.explanation: Geographic segmentation groups buyers by physical location, region, urban density, or climate.

pairs.match: A retail bank introduces a no-fee checking account tailored to university students aged 18 to 24.
pairs.explanation: Demographic segmentation groups buyers by observable statistics such as age, income, education, and household structure.

pairs.match: A travel company designs wilderness expeditions for consumers who value adventure and environmental stewardship.
pairs.explanation: Psychographic segmentation groups buyers by psychological traits, values, interests, and lifestyles.

pairs.match: A coffee roaster sends a bulk refill offer to customers who order beans every two weeks.
pairs.explanation: Behavioral segmentation groups buyers by observed actions such as usage frequency, occasion, and brand loyalty.

prompt: For each person highlighted below, identify whether they act only as the customer, only as the consumer, or as both.

cases.text: Maya pays at the pet store for a bag of grain-free dog food for her golden retriever.
cases.explanation: Maya purchases and pays for the dog food, while her dog is the consumer that eats it.

cases.text: Leo, an eighteen-month-old child, eats the organic applesauce his father bought at the supermarket.
cases.explanation: Leo uses and experiences the product, while his father was the customer who paid for it.

cases.text: Sam buys a hot espresso at the station kiosk and drinks it on the morning train.
cases.explanation: Sam both pays for the espresso (customer) and drinks it himself (consumer).

cases.text: A clinic administrator orders and pays for twenty ergonomic keyboards for the nursing staff.
cases.explanation: The administrator executes the purchase, while the nursing staff are the users who consume the keyboards.

prompt: A family is purchasing a new dishwasher. Match each decision role with the family member who performs it.

pairs.match: An older teenager points out that the current dishwasher leaves dishes wet and suggests replacing it.
pairs.explanation: The initiator is the person who first recognizes an unmet need or proposes acquiring a product.

pairs.match: One parent bookmarks three energy-efficient models and only prints those brochures for the family to review.
pairs.explanation: The gatekeeper or information gatherer controls the flow of product information that reaches the group.

pairs.match: An uncle who repairs appliances recommends choosing a stainless-steel tub over a plastic tub.
pairs.explanation: The influencer provides recommendations, expertise, or preferences that sway how alternatives are evaluated.

pairs.match: The other parent completes the checkout on the appliance store website using her credit card.
pairs.explanation: The buyer executes the transaction and pays for the item.

pairs.match: Every member of the household loads dishes into the machine and runs it after dinner.
pairs.explanation: The user consumes the product and judges its performance in daily life.

prompt: Sort each purchasing description into the assumptions of the classical rational economic model or bounded rationality and psychological influences.

cards.text: A buyer inspects every television sold in the city and calculates a weighted utility score for each attribute.
cards.explanation: The classical economic model assumes complete information and exhaustive computation across all options.

cards.text: A shopper's preference between two insurance plans remains identical regardless of how the deductible is worded.
cards.explanation: The classical model assumes stable preferences that do not shift with message framing.

cards.text: Pressed for time after work, a shopper grabs the familiar blue box of pasta without checking competing prices.
cards.explanation: Bounded rationality and brand familiarity allow shoppers to repeat satisfactory past choices under time limits.

cards.text: After a stressful exam, a student buys a premium dessert she would normally skip.
cards.explanation: Emotional states alter how buyers evaluate product attractiveness and spending.

cards.text: A new employee buys the same style of rain jacket worn by colleagues in his department.
cards.explanation: Social context shapes choices because consumers seek approval from peers.

prompt: A runner delegates buying replacement running shoes to an AI shopping agent. Sort each action by whether it is performed by the human consumer or the AI shopping agent.

cards.text: Specifies the goal of finding stability running shoes for flat feet under 120 dollars.
cards.explanation: In delegated shopping, the human consumer recognizes the need and specifies the goal and constraints.

cards.text: Queries six online shoe catalogs and extracts arch-support specifications and customer review scores.
cards.explanation: The AI shopping agent queries retail databases and reads product attributes and customer reviews.

cards.text: Narrows forty listings to the best matching pair in stock and submits the order within the budget limit.
cards.explanation: The AI agent filters alternatives and executes the transaction on the buyer's behalf.

cards.text: Runs ten kilometers in the delivered shoes and evaluates whether the cushioning prevents arch pain.
cards.explanation: The human consumer remains the final user who experiences the product after delivery.

prompt: Match each dark pattern with the interface design that exemplifies it.

pairs.match: A concert ticket site advertises seats at 60 dollars and reveals a mandatory 22-dollar service fee only on the final payment step.
pairs.explanation: Drip pricing conceals mandatory fees until the final checkout screen after the shopper has invested time.

pairs.match: A pop-up decline button reads: No thanks, I prefer paying full price and wasting money.
pairs.explanation: Confirmshaming uses guilt-inducing language on opt-out buttons to pressure users into accepting an offer.

pairs.match: A streaming trial starts with one click online, but canceling requires calling a support line during weekday business hours.
pairs.explanation: Roach-motel designs make signing up effortless while making cancellation slow and difficult.

pairs.match: A product page displays a ten-minute countdown timer that resets to ten minutes every time the browser page is refreshed.
pairs.explanation: False scarcity and countdown timers fabricate urgency to prevent consumers from comparing alternatives.
